verified.notes: Checked 15 Nov 2026 (checker agent, three passes). First pass: Livy and Dionysius accurate; fixed the 'muster' option (attested-advice to counterfactual: Livy 10.13.2–4 is a rumoured reproach after the event), three places where the scene's voice identified the army Fulvius beat with the army sent into Lucania (Livy does not say which), the Dionysius dating argument (the Postumius excerpt comes from a different collection; replaced by DH 17/18.1.2 on the Lucanians' broken agreements, Livy 8.25.3, 8.27.2, 8.27.9), the cognomen (Livy never calls the consul of 298 Barbatus; his only Cornelius Barbatus is the pontifex maximus of 304, 9.46.6), card-epitaph-3's accusative reading of Samnio (cut, unsupported), Livy's Lucanians offering rather than giving hostages, Volumnius suppressing the 296 risings through Fabius (10.18.8), an added 'ne' in the Italian of the epitaph, and smaller wording. Second and third passes confirmed these. Epitaph: by Matthew's decision the text is Orelli no. 550 as printed in Smith's Dictionary, attributed as such in r2-2's note and the source label; Smith prints LOVCANA, and Sandys' facsimile at 500 px shows a stroke after it that may be a final M; a 2005 article title (Ferone, Klio 87) reads 'Loucanam' but was not opened. EDR, EDCS and the JRS 2025 article 'Hoc Saxsum' were not opened, so the stone's reading, the lid/chest assignment and the CIL I², ILS and ILLRP numbers are not given; the CIL VI 1284–1285 pair is cited for the monument as listed on Commons. The ς/Ω sigla at 10.13.3 were not checked against the OCT preface; the note says only what the apparatus marks. Researcher's draft notes (2026-11-15). Livy cited by the Conway–Walters (OCT) section numbers in Perseus lat3 (books 1–10), checked against lat4 (same text and apparatus for book 10) and Weissenborn–Müller (lat2); book 40 only in lat2 (Weissenborn–Müller). Roberts 1912 (Perseus eng3) numbers 10.11–10.12 one section later than the OCT (his 10.11.10 begins with the consuls' election, OCT 10.11.10; his 10.12.2–3 = OCT 10.12.2; his 10.12.9 = OCT 10.12.8 end and 10.12.9). Roberts is not quoted anywhere in this scene, since his renderings are loose or open to question at each passage used: at 10.12.2 he renders 'haud inviolatos abituros' as 'their inviolability would be no longer respected' and 'in Samnio concilium' as 'any of the Samnite councils'; at 10.12.9 he has Fulvius 'sought a brilliant action' (for 'clara pugna … fuit') and 'carried Bovianum by storm' (a construal of 'Bovianum inde adgressus … vi cepit'; we take 'cepit' with Aufidena only); at 10.13.3 he adds 'only' and renders magistratus as 'government'; at 40.38.2 he prints 'Taurania' for 'Taurasinorum' and adds 'Anidus' at 40.38.3; at 40.38.6 he adds 'denarii'; at his 10.11.13 the OCR has 'it' for 'if'. English is therefore ours throughout. Perseus OCR and layout fixes: lat3 interleaves the OCT margin 'A.U.C. 456' in 10.12.2 and the apparatus note 'increpari s: increpare W.' in 10.13.3, both removed; lat3 'Cn . Fulvi' (10.12.9) closed up; lat2 'f/terat' for 'fuerat' (40.38.3); lat3 'haud baud' (8.39.12, 10.16.5; not quoted). Dionysius, Roman Antiquities, from Perseus grc2 (ed. K. Jacoby, Teubner 1885–1905): the excerpts are numbered there 17/18.1.1–3.1, with the alternative numbering 16.11–16.14 given as milestones; the file marks their source 'Ursin.'. ⟨τὴν⟩ in 17/18.3.1 is printed in the file as an editorial addition. No Dionysius translation was used; English and Italian ours. That the Dionysius excerpt concerns 298 is our inference (the excerpt has no date; see r1-3). Epitaph text as printed in capitals from Orelli no. 550 in Smith's Dictionary (Perseus, 1873 printing), compared with J. E. Sandys' facsimile ('Epigraphy', in A Companion to Latin Studies, 1913) as reproduced on Wikimedia Commons (File:Sepolcro scipioni, iscrizione A, scipione barbato.gif, public domain; viewed at 500 px). Smith prints LOVCANA; the facsimile, at 500 px, shows a stroke after it that may be a final M, so the two copies are not known to agree letter for letter. Punctuation in our 'la' is editorial and Smith's four-line division is given in the note. CIL numbers are those listed on the Commons category record for the sarcophagus (CIL VI 1284, 1285, 31587, 31588, 37039a; AE 1991, 71; AE 1997, 129); we did not open CIL, ILS or ILLRP, so we do not say which number is the lid and which the chest, and the CIL I², ILS and ILLRP numbers are not given. The Commons photograph of the inscription was too small to read the letters, so the text rests on Smith's printing, compared with Sandys' facsimile. Ager', 403292 Volaterrae); pleiades.stoa.org not opened. No decision uses the map: d1 is not geographic, and in d2 only one option has a place on the samnium map (Lucania lies south of its bounds). Not reachable this session, so not used or cited: attalus.org, LacusCurtius (Cassius Dio and Zonaras), Wikipedia, EDCS, EDR, Vatican Museums, the Köln server (Rheinisches Museum), JSTOR, Persée, archive.org, livius.org. Years BC are the conventional ones; Livy's sequence of consular years (298 Scipio–Fulvius, 297 Fabius–Decius, 296 Claudius–Volumnius) is the basis for 'last year' and 'two years later'. Decisions: d1 has Livy's version, Dionysius' version and one counterfactual; d2 has the historical choice (as the reproach reported at Rome gives it), and two counterfactuals, one built on that reproach.

blocks.text: Samnium, 298 BC. Your army is in Lucania, laying the land waste.
blocks.note: In Livy this comes in the Lucanian envoys' complaint at Rome. Dionysius' excerpt, which has no date, has the Samnites invade Lucania and win every battle; see the card Dionysius' excerpt.

blocks.text: Rome is at war in Etruria. Last year the Picentes, Rome's new allies, told Rome that the Samnites were looking to arms and a renewed war, and had sounded them out.

Lucanian envoys have been at Rome. They complained that you had tried to draw them by offers into an alliance in arms and, when they would not come, had invaded their land to force them by war into war. They asked to be taken under Rome's protection and offered hostages. The Senate's debate was short: a treaty with the Lucanians, and restitution to be demanded of the Samnites.
Now fetiales are on the road, sent to order you out of the land of Rome's allies and to take your army out of Lucanian territory.
The game seats you among the elders of the touto, whose counsel the magistrates ask.

steps.prompt: Roman fetiales are coming to order your army out of Lucania. What answer should they get?

options.label: Send men to meet them on the road. Tell them that if they come to any council in Samnium, they will not leave it unharmed.
options.kind_note: What the Samnites did, in Livy's version

consequence.text: Men go out to meet the fetiales on the way, with just that warning.

quote.la: fetiales missi, qui Samnitem decedere agro sociorum ac deducere exercitum finibus Lucanis iuberent; quibus obviam missi ab Samnitibus, qui denuntiarent, si quod adissent in Samnio concilium, haud inviolatos abituros.
quote.en: Fetiales were sent to order the Samnites to leave the land of Rome's allies and to take their army out of Lucanian territory. Men sent by the Samnites met them, to give them notice that if they came to any council in Samnium they would not go away inviolate.
quote.it: Furono mandati i feziali a intimare ai Sanniti di lasciare il territorio degli alleati e di ritirare l'esercito dal territorio lucano; andarono loro incontro inviati dei Sanniti, a dichiarare che, se si fossero presentati a una qualunque assemblea nel Sannio, non se ne sarebbero andati inviolati.

consequence.note: Roberts (his 10.12.2–3) has 'any of the Samnite councils' and 'their inviolability would be no longer respected'; the English is ours. Livy writes 'Samnitem', the Samnite, as a collective singular.

consequence.text: When this is heard at Rome, the Senate votes for war on the Samnites and the people order it.

options.label: Let them come before the common assembly, and answer them there: no treaty of ours binds us to take our friends and enemies at Rome's bidding.

consequence.text: In this account the Romans who come are not fetiales but envoys, the oldest and most honoured men of Rome, sent to the common assembly of the Samnites. They declare the Lucanians friends and allies of Rome, and ask you to give back the land you have taken from them and to commit no further act of war.
Your people hear them with anger and make their defence.

quote.la: οἱ δὲ Σαυνῖται τῶν πρέσβεων ἀκούσαντες ἠγανάκτουν τε καὶ ἀπελογοῦντο πρῶτον μὲν οὐκ ἐπὶ τούτῳ πεποιῆσθαι λέγοντες τὰς περὶ τῆς εἰρήνης ὁμολογίας, ἐπὶ τῷ μηδένα μήτε φίλον ἴδιον ἡγήσασθαι μήτʼ ἐχθρόν, ἐὰν μὴ Ῥωμαῖοι κελεύωσιν
quote.en: The Samnites, when they had heard the envoys, were indignant and made their defence, saying first that they had not made the peace agreements on condition that they should count no one their own friend or enemy unless the Romans bade them.
quote.it: I Sanniti, uditi gli ambasciatori, si indignarono e si difesero, dicendo anzitutto di non aver concluso gli accordi di pace a condizione di non ritenere nessuno amico o nemico proprio, se non per ordine dei Romani.

consequence.text: They add that Rome made the Lucanians its friends only lately, when they were already your enemies, and so contrived a pretext neither just nor decent for breaking the treaty.

The envoys reply that subjects who have agreed to follow, and ended the war on those terms, must obey in everything those who hold the leadership, and they threaten war if you will not do as you are told. Your people find the arrogance of Rome past bearing. They order the envoys to leave at once and vote to make ready for war, in common and city by city.

options.label: Hear them, and do what they ask. Bring the army home from Lucania and give back what it has taken.
options.kind_note: No Samnite is recorded proposing this in 298

consequence.text: It has been tried before. In the last war, the year before the Caudine Forks, your praetores, forced to bring the matter forward, decreed that Brutulus Papius, who had beyond doubt broken the last truce, be handed over to Rome with all the Roman booty and the prisoners, and that whatever the fetiales had demanded under the treaty be restored.
Brutulus took his own life. Fetiales took his body to Rome, with his goods.
Rome kept only the prisoners and whatever of the booty it recognised.

quote.la: nihil tamen earum rerum praeter captivos ac si qua cognita ex praeda sunt acceptum est; ceterarum rerum inrita fuit deditio.
quote.en: Yet of all this nothing was accepted except the prisoners and whatever of the booty was recognised; for the rest, the surrender was void.
quote.it: Tuttavia di tutto ciò non fu accettato nulla, tranne i prigionieri e quanto del bottino fu riconosciuto; per il resto la consegna fu vana.

consequence.note: Roberts adds 'by the Romans' and 'by the owners'; the English is ours.

consequence.text: Whether Rome would have taken the army's withdrawal as enough in 298, no source can tell us.

outcome.text: In Livy, Samnite envoys met the fetiales on the road and warned them away from any council in Samnium, and Rome voted war. In Dionysius, Roman envoys were heard by the common assembly of the Samnites, answered and sent away, and the Samnites voted to make ready for war.

blocks.text: Rome voted war on the Samnites: the Senate voted for it and the people ordered it. The consuls divided the commands between them: Etruria fell to L. Cornelius Scipio, the Samnites to Cn. Fulvius, and each set out for his own war.

Livy and Dionysius differ on who came and how far they got. Livy's fetiales are warned off on the road, before any council. Dionysius' envoys, the senior men of Rome, are heard by the common assembly of the Samnites and sent away.

Dionysius' excerpt has no date. That it tells of this year is our inference from its matter: a Samnite war renewed after a treaty, and Lucanians who know they have broken earlier agreements of friendship and alliance with Rome, beaten by the Samnites and sending hostages to Rome. Rome's first alliance with the Lucanians and their break with it fall in 326; Livy's Lucanians of 298 admit they had once erred enough and more.

Dionysius reckoned help for the Lucanians only the open pretext, one decent to give out to all. The hidden cause, in his judgement, was the power of the Samnites: great already, and expected to grow if the Lucanians were subdued and their neighbours followed.
War is voted. Scipio has gone to Etruria. Fulvius is coming into Samnium.
Your army is in Lucania.
blocks.note: Later in the year rumour at Rome speaks of an army raised against the Lucanians being thrown against Rome (Livy 10.13.3); Livy does not say which Samnite army met Fulvius. See d2.

steps.prompt: The consul Fulvius is coming. What should the magistrates do with the army that went into Lucania?

options.label: Turn it on the consul now, and meet him in Samnium.
options.kind_note: What the magistrates did, as the reproach reported at Rome has it

consequence.text: A Samnite army meets Fulvius near Bovianum and is beaten. The consul then attacks Bovianum, and not long after takes Aufidena by storm.

quote.la: Cn. Fulvi consulis clara pugna in Samnio ad Bovianum haudquaquam ambiguae victoriae fuit. Bovianum inde adgressus nec ita multo post Aufidenam vi cepit.
quote.en: The consul Cn. Fulvius fought a famous battle in Samnium near Bovianum, and the victory was in no way doubtful. He then attacked Bovianum, and not long after took Aufidena by storm.
quote.it: Il console Cn. Fulvio combatté nel Sannio presso Boviano una battaglia famosa, di vittoria per nulla incerta. Poi, attaccata Boviano, non molto tempo dopo prese d'assalto Aufidena.

consequence.note: Roberts (his 10.12.9) has Fulvius 'sought a brilliant action' for 'clara pugna … fuit', which the Latin does not say, and 'carried Bovianum by storm', one construal of 'Bovianum inde adgressus … vi cepit'. We take 'cepit' with Aufidena only, so whether Bovianum fell is left to inference. The English is ours.

consequence.text: Fulvius triumphs over the Samnites. Later in the year rumour reaches Rome that your magistrates are being reproached at home.

quote.la: increpari magistratus Samnitium, quod exercitum adversus Lucanum hostem comparatum obiecerint Romanis
quote.en: that the Samnite magistrates were being reproached for having thrown against the Romans an army raised against the Lucanian enemy
quote.it: che i magistrati sanniti venivano rimproverati per aver gettato contro i Romani un esercito allestito contro il nemico lucano

consequence.note: Reported as rumour ('fama exorta', 10.13.2). The Oxford text prints 'increpari', the reading its apparatus marks ς, against the manuscripts' 'increpare' (Ω); Weissenborn–Müller also print 'increpari'. Roberts adds 'only' and has 'government' for magistratus; the English is ours.

options.label: Do not throw an army raised for Lucania at Rome. Raise the whole strength of Samnium, and of our friends, first.
options.kind_note: No Samnite is recorded proposing this; built on the reproach reported at Rome

consequence.text: Later in the year, it is reported at Rome, your magistrates are reproached for throwing at Rome an army raised against the Lucanians. Rumour has the Etruscans and the Samnites enrolling huge armies, and the enemy rising to war with their own strength and their allies'.

Two years later a Samnite army, driven out of its own land, marches into Etruria and demands a council of the Etruscan leaders. The argument given to the Samnites there: they had tried everything to bear the war with their own strength, and had tried the help of neighbouring peoples, which was of little weight.
Whether a larger army in 298 would have stopped Fulvius, no source can tell us.

options.label: Keep the army in Lucania and finish that war. Let the towns of Samnium hold the consul.
options.kind_note: No Samnite is recorded proposing this

consequence.text: In one account your army has been winning there: the Lucanians have lost every battle and many places, and fear for all the rest of their land.

Two years later there are risings in Lucania, led by plebeian and needy leaders. The consul Volumnius puts them down through Q. Fabius, sent as proconsul with his old army, with the full goodwill of the Lucanian optimates.
Whether the towns of Samnium could have held without the army, or Lucania been won back, no source can tell us.

outcome.text: In Livy the Samnites met Fulvius near Bovianum and were clearly beaten; he attacked Bovianum, took Aufidena by storm and triumphed over the Samnites. Later that year rumour at Rome had the Samnite magistrates blamed for throwing at Rome an army raised against the Lucanians.

blocks.text: In Etruria, Scipio met the enemy drawn up for battle near Volaterrae. They fought most of the day with heavy losses on both sides; in the night the Etruscans left their camp, and he took it. He then laid their land waste with fire and sword, but left alone the cities in which they had taken refuge.
That is Livy's year. Scipio's own epitaph, cut on the front of his sarcophagus in the tomb of the Scipios, tells another story.
cites: Wikimedia Commons category record (Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus)

quote.la: Cornelius Lucius Scipio Barbatus, Gnaivod patre prognatus, fortis vir sapiensque, quoius forma virtutei parisuma fuit, consol, censor, aidilis quei fuit apud vos, Taurasia Cisauna Samnio cepit, subigit omne Loucana opsidesque abdoucit.
quote.en: Cornelius Lucius Scipio Barbatus, son of his father Gnaeus, a brave man and a wise, whose looks were the full match of his virtue; who was consul, censor and aedile among you. He took Taurasia and Cisauna in Samnium; he subdued all Lucania and led away hostages.
quote.it: Cornelio Lucio Scipione Barbato, nato dal padre Gneo, uomo forte e saggio, il cui aspetto fu in tutto pari al suo valore; fu presso di voi console, censore ed edile. Prese Taurasia e Cisauna nel Sannio; sottomise tutta la Lucania e portò via ostaggi.

blocks.note: Text as printed from Orelli no. 550 in Smith's Dictionary; punctuation ours. Smith divides it into four lines ending PATRE, PARISVMA, CISAVNA and ABDOVCIT. We have not opened a modern edition. Smith prints LOVCANA; Sandys' facsimile, at the size we could view it, shows a stroke after it that may be a final M. 'In Samnium' follows Smith's reading of Samnio; see the card The epitaph.

blocks.text: Both cannot be the whole story. Livy puts Scipio in Etruria and Fulvius in Samnium, gives Fulvius the victory near Bovianum, Aufidena and the triumph over the Samnites, and has the Lucanians offer hostages of their own accord. The epitaph gives no year, says nothing of Etruria, and credits Scipio with two Samnite towns that Livy's account of these years does not name, with all Lucania, and with hostages led away.

Smith's Dictionary set the two side by side and reported Niebuhr's view: the conquests in Samnium belong to 297, when Livy has a Scipio serving in Samnium as Fabius' legate. We have opened no modern study of the conflict.
cites: Smith, Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1873 printing), s.v. Scipio no. 5
blocks.note: Smith writes 'Samnium and Apulia'; the epitaph names Lucania. Niebuhr's History of Rome, which Smith cites as vol. iii pp. 363–366 and 378, was not opened.

blocks.text: The sarcophagus of L. Cornelius Scipio Barbatus, from the tomb of the Scipios on the Via Appia, now in the Vatican Museums (Museo Pio-Clementino), photographed in 2009. The epitaph runs across the front of the chest below the frieze.
cites: Wikimedia Commons category record (Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus)

figure.alt: A long grey stone chest against a red wall. Its lid ends in a large volute at each end; below a row of dentils runs a Doric frieze of triglyphs and rosettes, and under it four faint lines of inscription cross the front. The chest stands on a base of squared blocks with a one-line inscription, and an inscribed slab hangs on the wall above.
figure.credit: Photo: Bahnmoeller, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons; resized.

blocks.text: The sarcophagus comes from the tomb of the Scipios on the Via Appia and is now in the Vatican Museums. The Commons record of it notes a painted inscription on the lid as well as the one cut in archaic Latin on the chest, and lists it under CIL VI 1284 and 1285. Smith printed the chest's text from Orelli's collection, no. 550.
cites: Wikimedia Commons category record (Sarcophagus of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus)
Smith, Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1873 printing), s.v. Scipio no. 5
blocks.note: We have not opened CIL, ILS or ILLRP, so we do not say which CIL number is the lid and which the chest.

blocks.text: The spelling is old. Smith's normalised text sets the printed Gnaivod, quoius, virtutei, aidilis, quei, opsides and abdoucit beside Cnaeo, cujus, virtuti, aedilis, qui, obsides and abducit, and Loucana beside Lucaniam.
cites: Smith, Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1873 printing), s.v. Scipio no. 5

blocks.text: In the printed text final m is not written in Taurasia, Cisauna or omne; Smith restores it in each and reads Samnio as '(in) Samnio', in Samnium. How Samnio should be construed is not settled in anything we have opened.
cites: Smith, Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1873 printing), s.v. Scipio no. 5

blocks.text: The epitaph names its man with the family name first, Cornelius Lucius. In Sandys' facsimile the first line alone is set in from the left.
cites: Sandys, 'Epigraphy', in A Companion to Latin Studies (1913), facsimile on Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text: Livy's L. Cornelius Scipio, consul in 298, fights in Etruria, near Volaterrae and then in Etruscan land; Livy gives the Samnite command and the triumph over the Samnites to his colleague Fulvius.

Livy never gives the consul of 298 the cognomen Barbatus, which the epitaph gives; his only Cornelius Barbatus is the pontifex maximus of 304. He names a Scipio again in later years: in 297 a legate Scipio, ordered to lead the hastati of the first legion round, unseen, onto the nearest hills and show himself in the enemy's rear; in 295 L. Scipio as propraetor in command of the camp at Clusium; and in 293 an L. Scipio commanding the left wing at Aquilonia, who led the storm of the town gate with his shield held over his head.
Smith's Dictionary takes all of these to be Barbatus, the consul of 298. Livy himself does not say so.
cites: Smith, Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1873 printing), s.v. Scipio no. 5

blocks.text: Named positions we have opened: Livy, who gives Scipio Etruria in 298; the epitaph, which gives him two Samnite towns, all Lucania and hostages, with no year; and Niebuhr as Smith reports him, who put the Samnite conquests in 297, when Scipio was Fabius' legate.
cites: Smith, Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1873 printing), s.v. Scipio no. 5

blocks.text: Livy's Lucanians offer hostages of their own accord at the start of 298, and two years later the consul Volumnius puts down risings in Lucania through Q. Fabius. Neither passage names Scipio. We have opened no study that dates the epitaph's subjection of Lucania.

cards.title: Taurasia, Cisauna and the land of the Taurasini

blocks.text: Neither town has a known site. Pleiades lists Taurasia as unlocated in the Barrington Atlas, and describes Cisauna only as a site in Samnium taken by Scipio Barbatus, with no position.

Much later, in the year of the consuls A. Postumius and C. Calpurnius, the former consuls P. Cornelius and M. Baebius moved the Ligures Apuani down from their mountains. Livy says where they were sent.

quote.la: ager publicus populi Romani erat in Samnitibus, qui Taurasinorum fuerat.
quote.en: There was public land of the Roman people among the Samnites, which had belonged to the Taurasini.
quote.it: C'era presso i Sanniti un agro pubblico del popolo romano, che era appartenuto ai Taurasini.

blocks.note: Weissenborn–Müller text (Perseus lat2), whose OCR has 'f/terat' for 'fuerat'. Roberts prints 'Taurania'; the English is ours.

blocks.text: Livy gives about forty thousand free persons, with women and children, moved at public cost, and 150,000 of silver to equip their new homes; he does not name the unit.
Pliny lists Ligures called Corneliani and Baebiani among the inland communities of the second region, with the Hirpini.

Pleiades records the Barrington Atlas placing an ager Taurasinus, with a query. Whether Livy's Taurasini were the people of the epitaph's Taurasia, and whether their land became Rome's through Scipio, Livy does not say.
Aufidena, which Livy has Fulvius take by storm, is placed by Pleiades; Pliny lists the Aufidenates among the Samnites of the fourth region.

This passage survives as an excerpt, without a date. It tells how the Samnite war flared up again: soon after their treaty with Rome, the Samnites marched on the Lucanians, their neighbours, out of an old enmity.
blocks.note: Jacoby's numbering; the Perseus file also gives an alternative numbering, 16.11–16.14, for 17/18.1.1–3.1, and marks the source of the excerpts 'Ursin.'.

blocks.text: The two accounts give different motives for the invasion. Livy's Lucanian envoys say the Samnites invaded to force them into the war; Dionysius gives old enmity.

In Dionysius the Lucanians lost every battle and many places, and feared for all the rest of their land. Knowing they had broken their earlier agreements of friendship and alliance with Rome, they sent the noblest children from every city as hostages with their envoys. The Senate accepted the hostages and the friendship, and the people confirmed it.
blocks.note: Jacoby deletes τῆς before πόλεως (17/18.1.2), giving 'from every city'.

blocks.text: His verdict on the war's causes:

quote.la: ἡ μὲν δὴ φανερὰ τοῦ Σαυνιτικοῦ πολέμου πρόφασις καὶ πρὸς ἅπαντας εὐπρεπὴς λέγεσθαι ἡ Λευκανῶν ἐγένετο βοήθεια τῶν καταφυγόντων ἐπʼ αὐτούς … ἡ δʼ ἀφανὴς καὶ μᾶλλον αὐτοὺς ἀναγκάζουσα διαλύεσθαι ⟨τὴν⟩ φιλίαν ἡ τῶν Σαυνιτῶν ἰσχὺς πολλή τʼ ἤδη γεγονυῖα καὶ ἔτι πλείων γενήσεσθαι νομιζομένη
quote.en: The open pretext for the Samnite war, and one decent to give out to all, was help for the Lucanians, who had fled to them for refuge … The hidden cause, and the one that did more to compel them to dissolve the friendship, was the power of the Samnites, already great and thought likely to grow greater still.
quote.it: Il pretesto palese della guerra sannitica, e decoroso da dichiarare a tutti, fu l'aiuto ai Lucani, che si erano rifugiati presso di loro … La causa nascosta, e quella che più li costringeva a sciogliere l'amicizia, fu la potenza dei Sanniti, già grande e che si riteneva sarebbe cresciuta ancora.

blocks.note: ⟨τὴν⟩ is an editorial addition in the Perseus text of Jacoby. The omitted words say this was treated as a common, ancestral custom of Rome: to help those who are wronged and take refuge with it.

blocks.text: He ends: the treaty was broken as soon as the envoys arrived, and two armies were enrolled. The excerpt does not say whose.
Livy records that the old treaty was given back to the Samnites at the end of the last war. He does not give its terms.

In Dionysius the two sides read the peace differently. The Samnites say they never agreed to count no one friend or enemy except at Rome's order. Rome's envoys answer that the Samnites are subjects who agreed to follow, ended the war on those terms, and must obey in everything those who hold the leadership.

Two years later in Etruria, as the argument is given to Livy's Samnites, they had sued for peace when they could not bear the war, and taken up war again because peace with servitude was heavier than war with freedom.

Livy describes the rite for demanding redress. The envoy, his head veiled, states Rome's demands at the enemy's border, then again to the first man he meets, again entering the gate, and again entering the forum.

If what is demanded is not handed over in thirty-three days, the envoy declares the people unjust and returns to Rome. Once war is voted, a fetialis carries a spear to the enemy's border and throws it into their land before at least three grown men.

The rite as Livy sets it out under Ancus Marcius: the demand spoken at the border, on crossing it, to the first man met, at the gate and in the forum; thirty-three days; the envoy's return to Rome and the king's question to the patres; then the spear, 'ferratam aut praeustam sanguineam', thrown into their land before at least three grown men. A diagram of his words. Ours: the figures, the town and the layout; of the envoy's dress Livy gives only the woollen fillet covering his head. He tells it as the form first used against the Latins. For 298 he reports only the demand, the Samnite warning and the votes, so this is not a picture of that embassy.

figure.alt: Diagram in seven numbered stations. One to four: an envoy with covered head speaks at a border line, to the first man he meets, at a town gate and in the forum. Five: a row of thirty-three strokes for thirty-three days. Six: a king puts the question to a row of senators in order. Seven: a fetialis throws a spear across a border line while three men look on; below, two spears, one iron-tipped and one with a fire-hardened point. Latin labels quote Livy at each station.

blocks.text: For 298 Livy reports only the Senate's vote that restitution be demanded, the order the fetiales were sent to give, the Samnite warning, and the votes of the Senate and the people. He says nothing of thirty-three days or a spear, and does not say whether the fetiales spoke their demand.
Livy gives the Samnites fetiales of their own. In the last war, the year before the Caudine Forks, it was fetiales sent by the Samnite decree who carried the body of Brutulus Papius to Rome.
Livy's Lucanians first made a treaty with Rome in the opening year of the last war, together with the Apuli.

Soon after, roused by young men who had been bribed, had beaten one another with rods and claimed the Roman consuls had done it, the Lucanians renewed their alliance with the Samnites. The Samnites made them give hostages and take Samnite garrisons. The authors of the false charge then moved to Tarentum, and Livy puts the plot down to the Tarentines.
In 298 the Lucanians, saying they had once erred enough and more, offered Rome hostages. In Dionysius' undated excerpt they were the noblest children from every city, and the Senate accepted them.
blocks.note: Jacoby deletes τῆς before πόλεως in Dionysius 17/18.1.2, giving 'from every city'; with it the words would mean 'from the whole city'.

blocks.text: The epitaph has Scipio subdue all Lucania and lead hostages away. It does not say from whom, or when.
